entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: One conversation centered on the ever accelerating progress of technology and changes in the mode of human life, which gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue.
entries.work: “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64:3, Part 2
entries.caution: Ulam’s own sentence, not von Neumann’s: Ulam writes it in his own voice, recalling what a conversation was about. Only the preceding sentence (“The interests of humanity may change…”) is a direct quotation of von Neumann. The 2012 Kurzweil foreword to the Science, Computers, and People reprint carries the misattribution. Printed-text traps: no hyphen in “ever accelerating”; it reads “in the history of the race,” not “of the human race”; “as we know them” is often dropped. It appears once in the article, in the personal-recollection section; Ulam supplies no date for the conversation. Cite the Bulletin, not the SCP reprint.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: The interests of humanity may change, the present curiosities in science may cease, and entirely different things may occupy the human mind in the future.
entries.work: quoted in Ulam, “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64:3, Part 2
entries.caution: Reported speech: Ulam quotes it in a memorial article, with no date for the occasion.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: He began to work on the theory of computing and planned the work, to remain unfinished, on the theory of automata. It was at the outset of such studies that his interest in the working of the nervous system and the schematized properties of organisms claimed so much of his attention.
entries.work: “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64:3, Part 2
entries.caution: OCR spacing artifacts in the AMS scan (“t h a t” for “that”) were closed by the compiler; nothing else altered. Cite the Bulletin, not the SCP ch. 16 reprint.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: It was toward the end of his life that he felt sure enough of himself to engage freely and yet painstakingly in the creation of a possible new mathematical discipline. This was to be a combinatorial theory of automata and organisms. His illness and premature death permitted him to make only a beginning.
entries.work: “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64:3, Part 2
entries.caution: Cite the Bulletin, not the SCP reprint. The report quotes this immediately after the preceding passage; in the original the two are separated by a paragraph.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: We decided to look for ways to find, as it were, homomorphic images of the given physical problem in a mathematical schema which could be represented by a system of fictitious ‘particles’ treated by an electronic computer.
entries.work: “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64:3, Part 2
entries.caution: OCR rendered “n-dimensional” as “w-dimensional” later in the same passage and was corrected by the compiler; this sentence extracted clean.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: After the end of the war, he would express sentiments, somewhat similar to remarks reportedly made by Einstein, that the bewildering wealth of nuclear and elementary particle physics make premature any attempt to formulate a general quantum theory of fields, at least for the time being.
entries.work: “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64:3, Part 2
entries.caution: Doubly indirect: Ulam reports von Neumann’s sentiments, and reports them as “somewhat similar” to remarks “reportedly made by” Einstein.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: To my mind and to my taste, the most important work he did is what he did when he was getting older, which mathematicians don’t appreciate, namely his speculations on automata, on the brain, and his contributions to computing and to problems in hydrodynamics.
entries.work: “Conversations with Rota,” Los Alamos Science, Special Issue No. 15
entries.caution: A tape transcribed and edited by Françoise Ulam and further edited by Los Alamos Science. The LANL text extraction carries hyphenation and ligature artifacts, closed by the compiler. MacTutor reproduces the same conversation with minor editorial changes.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Mathematicians start with axioms whose validity they don’t question. You might say it is just a game — ‘the great game’ as Hilbert called it… Now to some extent, at least, I would claim that in physics the situation is inverse. Given a lot of facts, let’s call them theorems, we look for axioms, that is to say physical laws, from which they would follow. So physics is an inverse process.
entries.work: “Physics for Mathematicians,” Science, Computers, and People: From the Tree of Mathematics, ch. 2
entries.caution: The report marks its own elision with an ellipsis. Emphasis in the printed text is Ulam’s own underlining, preserved by the SCP editors; any bold in the report is the report’s. The on-disk SCP is a 26-page excerpt (front matter plus chs. 1–2), so SCP page numbers hold here but not for journal-sourced Ulam material.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: And in mathematics itself, you could think of such a game: Given some theorems in a certain well-defined notation or algebra, find the underlying axioms. This game has not been played and I’ll tell you why. It is because the idea of algorithm and the formalization of what we call definite equational theory is very new. So mathematicians have never hesitated to create objects of their own. Right now there begins to appear some work which I would consider of this inverse type; perhaps it was stimulated by the existence of computers.
entries.work: “Physics for Mathematicians,” Science, Computers, and People: From the Tree of Mathematics, ch. 2
entries.caution: Emphasis in the printed text is Ulam’s own underlining, preserved by the editors; bold in the report is the report’s own.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: In a sufficiently complicated problem, actual sampling is better than an examination of all the chains of possibilities…. It so happened that computing machines were coming into existence, and here was something suitable for machine calculation.
entries.work: Adventures of a Mathematician
entries.caution: Primary: the author holds his own scans of the physical book. The wording carried here was keyed from a secondary transcription (Gil Press, Substack) during extraction and has not yet been reconciled against those scans; the specific point to check is the singular/plural variant — some transcriptions read “all the chain of possibilities”.

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: The methods of analytical mechanics do not even give a qualitative survey of the behavior of a system of three mutually attractive bodies. Obviously the statistical-mechanical approach would also be unrealistic.
entries.work: “The Monte Carlo Method,” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44:247
entries.caution: The JASA source is an image scan OCR’d at 300 dpi by the compiler; garbles elsewhere in the article are marked [sic — OCR]; this passage extracted clean.

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: To calculate the probability of a successful outcome of a game of solitaire… is a completely intractable task. On the other hand, the laws of large numbers and the asymptotic theorems of the theory of probabilities will not throw much light even on qualitative questions concerning such probabilities. Obviously the practical procedure is to produce a large number of examples of any given game and then to examine the relative proportion of successes.
entries.work: “The Monte Carlo Method,” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44:247
entries.context: The ellipsis replaces the printed parenthesis: “(we understand here only such games where skill plays no role).”
entries.caution: OCR clean in this passage.

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: The classical methods for dealing with these equations are extremely laborious and incomplete in the sense that solutions in ‘closed form’ are unobtainable.
entries.work: “The Monte Carlo Method,” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44:247

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: we avoid dealing with multiple integrations… but instead sample single chains of events
entries.work: “The Monte Carlo Method,” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44:247
entries.context: The ellipsis removes “or multiplications of the probability matrices”. The full printed sentence begins “The essential feature of the process is that…”

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis
entries.quote: Stan’s extensive mathematical background made him aware that statistical sampling techniques had fallen into desuetude because of the length and tediousness of the calculations. But with this miraculous development of the ENIAC—along with the applications Stan must have been pondering—it occurred to him that statistical techniques should be resuscitated, and he discussed this idea with von Neumann. Thus was triggered the spark that led to the Monte Carlo method.
entries.work: “The Beginning of the Monte Carlo Method,” Los Alamos Science, Special Issue No. 15
entries.caution: Written by Metropolis about Ulam in 1987, not Ulam’s own testimony. LANL PDF extraction with hyphenation artifacts closed.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: I have been thinking a good deal about the possibility of using statistical methods to solve neutron diffusion and multiplication problems, in accordance with the principle suggested by Stan Ulam. The more I think about this, the more I become convinced that the idea has great merit.
entries.work: letter to R. D. Richtmyer, reprinted in Analogies Between Analogies: The Mathematical Reports of S. M. Ulam and His Los Alamos Collaborators
entries.caution: Read in the open-access UC Press e-book reprint, not from the original letter.

entries.speaker: R. G. Schrandt and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Our examples show both the complexity and the richness of forms obtained from starting with a simple geometrical element and the application of a simple recursive rule. The amount of ‘information’ contained in these objects is therefore quite small, despite their apparent complexity and unpredictability.
entries.work: “On Recursively Defined Geometrical Objects and Patterns of Growth,” Los Alamos report LA-3762
entries.locus: concluding section; in Analogies Between Analogies, pp. 385–386
entries.caution: The report cites the Los Alamos report; the text was read in the 1990 UC Press reprint. The predecessor paper (Ulam, Proc. Symp. Appl. Math. 14, 1962) could not be obtained.

entries.speaker: R. G. Schrandt and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: It is not known whether some of these side branches will grow to infinite length or whether they will all in turn be choked off by other side branches growing from the stem at later times.
entries.work: “On Recursively Defined Geometrical Objects and Patterns of Growth,” Los Alamos report LA-3762
entries.caution: Read in the 1990 UC Press reprint, not the original laboratory report.

entries.speaker: Enrico Fermi, John Pasta and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: The results show very little, if any, tendency toward equipartition of energy among the degrees of freedom.
entries.work: “Studies of Nonlinear Problems,” Los Alamos report LA-1940
entries.locus: abstract; in Analogies Between Analogies, p. 139
entries.caution: Bold in the abstract is the source’s own. The original carries a footnote thanking Mary Tsingou for coding and running the computations.

entries.speaker: W. A. Beyer, M. L. Stein and Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: The notion of complexity, in our view, is separate from, though associated with the idea of the amount of information or entropy of a system.
entries.work: “The Notion of Complexity,” Los Alamos report LA-4822; in Analogies Between Analogies
entries.caution: Italics on “information” and “entropy” are the source’s. Read in the 1990 UC Press reprint, not the original laboratory report.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: Lastly, my main aim is actually to bring out a rather different aspect of the matter. I suspect that a deeper mathematical study of the nervous system… will affect our understanding of the aspects of mathematics itself that are involved. In fact, it may alter the way in which we look on mathematics and logics proper. I will try to explain my reasons for this belief later.
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain
entries.context: The ellipsis removes the printed parenthetical “—‘mathematical’ in the sense outlined above—”.
entries.caution: The working text is a pdftotext extraction of the Yale third edition (2012) whose ligature repair corrupts mathematics; prose extracted reliably, but any numeric passage must be re-checked against the page image.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: This conclusion was well worth working out just because of, rather than in spite of, its absolute implausibility.
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain
entries.caution: Italicised in the original; any bold in the report is the report’s own. Exponents in the surrounding precision figures did not survive text extraction.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: We have seen how this leads to a lower level of arithmetical precision but to a higher level of logical reliability: a deterioration in arithmetics has been traded for an improvement in logics.
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain
entries.caution: Bold in the report is the report’s own; the printing carries no emphasis here. Section heading: “Arithmetical Precision or Logical Reliability, Alternatives.”

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: It is only proper to realize that language is largely a historical accident… Just as languages like Greek or Sanskrit are historical facts and not absolute logical necessities, it is only reasonable to assume that logics and mathematics are similarly historical, accidental forms of expression. They may have essential variants, i.e. they may exist in other forms than the ones to which we are accustomed. Indeed, the nature of the central nervous system and of the message systems that it transmits indicate positively that this is so. We have now accumulated sufficient evidence to see that whatever language the central nervous system is using, it is characterized by less logical and arithmetical depth than what we are normally used to. The following is an obvious example of this: the retina of the human eye performs a considerable reorganization of the visual image as perceived by the eye. Now this reorganization is effected on the retina, or to be more precise, at the point of entry of the optic nerve by means of three successive synapses only, i.e. in terms of three consecutive logical steps… Consequently, there exist here different logical structures from the ones we are ordinarily used to in logics and mathematics… Thus logics and mathematics in the central nervous system, when viewed as languages, must structurally be essentially different from those languages to which our common experience refers.
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain, closing section “The Language of the Brain Not the Language of Mathematics”
entries.context: Elided text not recovered. The dossier records only that the cut included a sentence on the statistical character of the message system; the wording was not transcribed.
entries.caution: An earlier draft of the report carried an unmarked elision here; the passage is now quoted with ellipses marked. The printed heading is “The Language of the Brain Not the Language of Mathematics” — “not the language of arithmetic” is not the printed wording. The manuscript breaks off at p. 83.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: It also ought to be noted that the language here involved may well correspond to a short code in the sense described earlier, rather than to a complete code: when we talk mathematics, we may be discussing a secondary language, built on the primary language truly used by the central nervous system… However, the above remarks about reliability and logical and arithmetical depth prove that whatever the system is, it cannot fail to differ considerably from what we consciously and explicitly consider as mathematics.
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain, closing section “The Language of the Brain Not the Language of Mathematics”
entries.context: The ellipsis removes “Thus the outward forms of our mathematics are not absolutely relevant from the point of view of evaluating what the mathematical or logical language truly used by the central nervous system is.”

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: such memories, most characteristically designated as ‘memories made up from basic active organs,’ are, in every sense that matters, extremely expensive
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain, “The Underlying Componentry of the Memory Need Not Be the Same as That of the Basic Active Organs”
entries.caution: Numerals in the ENIAC figures that follow did not survive text extraction.

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: We do most emphatically not know what type of physical entities are the basic components for the memory in question.
entries.work: The Computer and the Brain

entries.speaker: John von Neumann
entries.quote: I doubt that any mathematician now living has much of a relationship to more than a quarter.
entries.work: “The Mathematician,” in R. B. Heywood (ed.), The Works of the Mind
entries.locus: pp. 180–196 (no page apparatus in the source transcription)
entries.caution: VERIFIED-AS-TRANSCRIPTION; the source transcription carries no page apparatus. A different statement from Ulam’s 1958 report of “one-third”.

entries.speaker: Klara von Neumann
entries.quote: By January 1956 Johnny was confined to a wheelchair, but still he attended meetings, was wheeled into his office, and continued working on the manuscript for the lecture… In spite of many efforts, Johnny could not finish writing his planned lectures in time; as a matter of tragic fate he could never finish writing them at all.
entries.work: preface to The Computer and the Brain (Yale)
entries.context: The ellipsis compresses two paragraphs. The printed text between them reads “Clearly his strength was waning from day to day; all trips and speaking engagements had to be canceled one by one, with this single exception—the Silliman Lectures.”
entries.caution: Pagination is from the Yale third edition (2012); the 1958 first edition has different front matter.

entries.speaker: Klara von Neumann
entries.quote: The unfinished manuscript of the Silliman Lectures went with him to the hospital, where he made a few more attempts to work on it; but by then the illness had definitely gained the upper hand, and even Johnny’s exceptional mind could not overcome the weariness of the body.
entries.work: preface to The Computer and the Brain (Yale)
entries.caution: Edition caveat as above. Von Neumann died 8 February 1957; the book was published posthumously in 1958.

entries.speaker: Albert Einstein
entries.quote: I consider it quite possible that physics cannot be based on the field concept, i.e., on continuous structures. In that case, nothing remains of my entire castle in the air, gravitation theory included, [and of] the rest of modern physics.
entries.work: letter to Michele Besso
entries.caution: Reaches this corpus through a secondary source: Bob Doyle, My God, He Plays Dice! (Information Philosopher), rather than the collected papers. The intermediary is identified and its rendering is the text quoted. The bracketed “[and of]” is that source’s interpolation.

entries.speaker: Albert Einstein
entries.quote: I must confess that I was not able to find a way to explain the atomistic character of nature. My opinion is that if the objective description through the field as an elementary concept is not possible, then one has to find a possibility to avoid the continuum (together with space and time) altogether. But I have not the slightest idea what kind of elementary concepts could be used in such a theory.
entries.work: letter to David Bohm
entries.caution: Reaches this corpus through the same identified secondary source as the Besso letter: Bob Doyle, My God, He Plays Dice! (Information Philosopher), rather than the collected papers.

entries.speaker: Albert Einstein
entries.quote: inconsistent with the principle that physics has to represent a reality in space and time without phantom actions over distances
entries.work: letter to Max Born, as translated by Born in his Waynflete Lectures
entries.caution: Read in Born’s Waynflete Lectures, in Born’s translation, so the English is Born’s rather than Einstein’s. Quoted as a sentence fragment inside the report’s prose.

entries.speaker: Richard Feynman
entries.quote: We can imagine that this complicated array of moving things which constitutes ‘the world’ is something like a great chess game being played by the gods, and we are observers of the game.
entries.work: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I

entries.speaker: Richard Feynman
entries.quote: has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery
entries.work: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. III
entries.caution: Quoted as a fragment inside the report’s own sentence; “only” is italicised in the original. The report does not give volume or section; the dossier does.

entries.speaker: Richard Feynman
entries.quote: None of them can get the right curve for P₁₂ in terms of P₁ and P₂.
entries.work: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. III
entries.caution: Two wordings exist: the dossier records the §1-1 form as “None of them has succeeded”; this is the §1-5 wording.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Philosophers and logicians, from Duns Scotus in the Twelfth Century to Ludwig Wittgenstein only yesterday, have done a lot of clear thinking about all this stuff. If your friends in AI persist in ignoring their past, they will be condemned to repeat it, at a high cost that will be borne by the taxpayers.
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: The twelfth-century dating of Duns Scotus (c. 1265–1308) is Rota’s own and appears in the 1997 Indiscrete Thoughts reprint. Ulam’s speech as reported by Rota, not a transcript. The source read is a re-keyed transcription of the 1985 journal printing with no page apparatus, so the citation is at article level. The essay has two 1985/1986 printings under different titles (Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2, 97–99; Physica D 22, 1–3) plus the 1997 book reprint.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: I now take this object out of my pocket and ask you to look at it. No amount of staring at this object will ever tell you that this is a key, unless you already have some previous familiarity with the way keys are used.
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: Ulam’s words as reported by Rota. Rota gives the same example in a Los Alamos Science dialogue months earlier, credited (“Let me give a simple example of context-dependence, due to Ulam”); Ulam raises “key, lock, labyrinth” on a 1974 tape. The wording here is Rota’s rendering. Transcription-level source, no page apparatus.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Now look at that man passing by in a car. How do you tell that it is not just a man you are seeing, but a passenger?
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: Reported speech via Rota; re-keyed transcription of the 1985 journal text, cited at article level only.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: When you write down precise definitions for these words, you discover that what you are describing is not an object, but a function, a role that is inextricably tied to some context. Take away the context, and the meaning also disappears.
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: Reported speech via Rota. A circulating secondary transcription of the Physica D printing garbles this line as “a role that is tied inextricably tied to some context”; the reading here is “inextricably tied.” Transcription-level source, no page apparatus.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Your friends in AI are now beginning to trumpet the role of contexts, but they are not practising their lesson. They still want to build machines that see by imitating cameras, perhaps with some feedback thrown in. Such an approach is bound to fail, since it starts out with a logical misunderstanding.
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: Reported speech via Rota. Note “practising” (British spelling) in this printing; a circulating secondary transcription reads “since it start out.” The 1997 book reprint uses “A.I.” house style, so wording differs by printing.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Logic formalizes only very few of the processes by which we actually think… What is it that you see when you see? You see an object as a key, you see a man in a car as a passenger, you see some sheets of paper as a book. It is the word ‘as’ that must be mathematically formalized, on a par with the connectives ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘implies’ and ‘not’…
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.context: The ellipses cut “The time has come to enrich formal logic by adding to it some other fundamental notions” and “that have already been accepted into a formal logic. Until you do that, you will not get very far with your AI problem.”
entries.caution: Reported speech via Rota. A 2026 secondary source renders the connectives with a serial comma and doubled quotation marks; the 1985 text does not.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Around the turn of the century, most mathematicians and physicists probably thought that the common-sense notion of simultaneity of events was an obvious one, and needed no exact explanation. Yet a few years later Einstein came out with his special theory of relativity, which exactly analyzed it. I see no reason why we shouldn’t do with ‘as’ what Einstein did with simultaneity.
entries.work: quoted in Gian-Carlo Rota, “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: Reported speech via Rota. Absent from the secondary record until the full essay text was obtained. Transcription-level source, article-level citation only.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: We never returned to this topic in our conversations, and since then, whenever I recall that day, I wonder whether or when AI will ever crash the barrier of meaning.
entries.work: “The Barrier of Meaning,” Letters in Mathematical Physics 10:2
entries.caution: The 1985 journal text reads “AI,” not “artificial intelligence”; the expanded form circulating in the literature is Melanie Mitchell’s expansion. Quoted here as a tail of a longer sentence. The preceding sentence in the essay prints “Charles Saunders Peirce” for Charles Sanders Peirce.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: In his fascination with physics, he was led to formulate mathematical thoughts that had a background of physics, but that bore the unmistakable ring of mathematics (he once started to draft a long paper which was to be titled ‘Physics for Mathematicians’). One of the most striking is his proposal for the reconstruction of the CGS system on the basis of random walk.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser)
entries.caution: The report cites the book without a page number; the passage sits in ch. VI, “The Lost Café,” pp. 64–85, read from a partial on-disk extraction whose text of that chapter truncates mid-sentence at p. 85.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Philosophers are needed today more than ever to tell the AI engineers some unpleasant truths. The philosopher’s role has always been that of stating facts that may have been on everybody’s mind but that no one dared state clearly. Eventually, engineers will reluctantly acknowledge that what the philosopher says is the truth, but they will then get rid of the philosopher.
entries.work: “Mathematics, Philosophy and Artificial Intelligence: A Dialogue with Gian-Carlo Rota and David Sharp,” Los Alamos Science No. 12
entries.context: The report cuts the example that follows, without an ellipsis: “In the early fifties engineers attempted to build a machine that translated from one language to another…”
entries.caution: Read via text extraction of the LANL PDF (LA-UR-85-2000); speaker labels are the source’s own.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Let me give a simple example of context-dependence, due to Ulam.
entries.work: “Mathematics, Philosophy and Artificial Intelligence: A Dialogue with Gian-Carlo Rota and David Sharp,” Los Alamos Science No. 12
entries.caution: Appears in a second, directly readable printing.

entries.speaker: Kenneth Baclawski, Gian-Carlo Rota and Stanley Billis

entries.speaker: Kenneth Baclawski, Gian-Carlo Rota and Stanley Billis
entries.quote: The four principal processes of probability theory are all determined by maximum entropy properties.
entries.work: Introduction to Probability Theory, ch. VIII, “Entropy and Information”

entries.quote: Like Veo, it doesn’t rely on a hard-coded physics engine; instead, DeepMind says, the model teaches itself how the world works.
entries.work: TechCrunch report on Genie 3
entries.caution: A journalist’s sentence, not Google’s own words. An earlier draft of the report presented it as a company statement and cut the interpolated “DeepMind says” without marking it; it is now attributed to TechCrunch.

entries.speaker: Alexandre LeBrun
entries.quote: My prediction is that ‘world models’ will be the next buzzword. In six months, every company will call itself a world model to raise funding.
entries.work: quoted in TechCrunch, on AMI Labs’ $1.03bn raise
entries.caution: Secondary reporting. Attributed in the piece to Alexandre LeBrun, not to Yann LeCun. LeCun’s A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence could not be retrieved (OpenReview returned HTTP 403); nothing is quoted from him directly.

entries.speaker: Skild AI
entries.quote: there is no Internet of robotics
entries.work: quoted in The Robot Report, on the $1.4bn raise and Skild Brain
entries.caution: Vendor statement relayed through trade press.

entries.speaker: LIBERO-PRO
entries.quote: although existing models achieve over 90% accuracy under the standard LIBERO evaluation, their performance collapses to 0.0% under our generalized setting.
entries.caution: Peer-reviewed. The accompanying figures — OpenVLA and π0 dropping to zero beyond 0.2-unit object-position shifts, π0.5 at 0.38 — are in the report’s citation line, not in the quotation.

entries.speaker: LIBERO-Plus
entries.quote: even without any valid language input, the performance of some models remained largely unchanged.
entries.work: LIBERO-Plus, CVPR 2026
entries.caution: Peer-reviewed; CVPR 2026 poster.

entries.speaker: Physics-IQ
entries.quote: visual realism does not imply physical understanding.
entries.work: Physics-IQ, arXiv:2501.09038
entries.caution: An earlier draft of the report misattributed Physics-IQ to Meta; it is not Meta’s, and its best scorer is OpenAI’s Sora at 29.5%. Per-model scores below Sora’s were read off a figure and are UNVERIFIED to the decimal (the leaderboard did not render on fetch). An earlier draft described the conclusion as “four words long”; it is seven.

entries.speaker: CausalVQA
entries.quote: Anticipation questions, in particular, are difficult for this pool of models, while easy for humans: the average model here scores 39.34% paired vs humans at 83.54%.
entries.work: CausalVQA, arXiv:2506.09943
entries.caution: Peer-reviewed. The benchmark is Meta’s own. The report quotes only the first clause.

entries.speaker: Meta AI (V-JEPA 2)
entries.quote: the JEPA approach focuses on learning representations for predictable aspects of a scene (e.g., the trajectory of an object in motion) while ignoring unpredictable details that generative objectives emphasize, since they make pixel-level predictions.
entries.work: V-JEPA 2, arXiv:2506.09985
entries.context: The printed sentence opens “In contrast to approaches based on video generation,…”, dropped without an ellipsis.
entries.caution: Preprint, not peer-reviewed.

entries.speaker: Meta AI
entries.quote: Before taking action, we use our world model to imagine the potential consequences.
entries.work: V-JEPA 2 launch blog post, ai.meta.com
entries.caution: Blog copy. A full-text search of the V-JEPA 2 paper for “imagine,” “imagination,” “mental,” “simulator” and “dream” returns no matching sentences.

entries.speaker: Meta AI
entries.quote: Our internal model of the world provides us with this intuition and also acts as an internal simulator, allowing us to predict the outcome of a hypothetical action.
entries.work: V-JEPA 2 launch blog post, ai.meta.com
entries.caution: Blog copy; the vocabulary is absent from the matching technical paper.

entries.speaker: Google DeepMind
entries.quote: AI systems that can use their understanding of the world to simulate aspects of it, enabling agents to predict both how an environment will evolve and how their actions will affect it.
entries.work: Genie 3 launch post, deepmind.google
entries.caution: Blog copy, not a paper.

entries.speaker: NVIDIA
entries.quote: Physical AI needs to be trained digitally first. It needs a digital twin of itself, the policy model, and a digital twin of the world, the world model.
entries.work: Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform, arXiv:2501.03575
entries.caution: Preprint, not peer-reviewed. “imagine,” “imagination” and “dreaming” do not appear anywhere in the Cosmos material examined; the term used is “digital twin.”

entries.speaker: Newton (Linux Foundation project)
entries.quote: a GPU-accelerated physics simulation engine built upon NVIDIA Warp, specifically targeting roboticists and simulation researchers
entries.work: Newton project documentation, github.com/newton-physics/newton
entries.caution: An earlier draft of the report absorbed the connective “emphasising” — the dossier chapter author’s word, outside the quotation marks — into the quotation. Newton was started by Disney Research, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA.

entries.speaker: Runway
entries.quote: A world model is an AI system that builds an internal representation of an environment and uses it to simulate future events within that environment.
entries.work: GWM-1 research post, runway.com
entries.caution: Research-blog copy.

entries.speaker: 1X
entries.quote: a computer program that can imagine how the world evolves in response to an agent’s behavior
entries.work: 1X World Model page, 1x.tech
entries.caution: Blog copy. The stated use of the 1X world model is evaluation.

entries.speaker: Physical Intelligence
entries.quote: The model first produces a high-level action expressed in language ... and then selects the motor commands using its flow matching action expert
entries.work: π0.5 blog post, pi.website
entries.context: Elided text not recovered; the ellipsis is the dossier’s cut, rendered as “…” in the report.
entries.caution: Blog copy. The phrase “world model” does not appear in the π0.5 abstract.

entries.speaker: Physical Intelligence
entries.quote: At runtime, the subgoal images are produced by a lightweight world model, which takes in the same subtask instruction
entries.caution: Preprint. Parameter counts and training-data volumes for π0.7 are not disclosed. A search of the π0.7 text for “imagine”/“imagination” returned no matches.

entries.speaker: Karcini, Mehrban, Nguyen, Schwager, Ajoundani, Cadena, Peters, Hutter and Bou-Ammar
entries.quote: Human motion, internet video, simulation rollouts, and interactive demonstrations contain rich information about tasks, goals, contacts, failures, and physical constraints, yet most of this information is not directly usable by robot policies because it lacks embodiment-specific action labels, task semantics, and reward structure.
entries.work: “Robots Need More than VLA and World Models,” arXiv:2606.06556
entries.context: A shortened span quoted inside the report’s prose, opening at “contain rich information…”
entries.caution: Peer-reviewed position paper.

entries.speaker: Google DeepMind (DreamerV3)
entries.quote: Dreamer learns a model of the environment and improves its behavior by imagining future scenarios
entries.work: DreamerV3, arXiv:2301.04104
